title: Calculating distance and area with a ratio scale

match.reason: No bank point teaches calculating distance and area from a ratio scale; the scale cards cover the geographic scale of an issue (local to global), which is a different idea, and the map-scale card lacks the area-by-grid-squares content.

draft.title: Distance and area with a ratio scale
card: A ratio scale such as 1:25,000 means one unit on the map is 25,000 of the same unit on the ground. So 1 cm on the map is 25,000 cm on the ground, which is 250 m.
To find a distance, measure it on the map in centimetres. Then multiply by the ground distance for 1 cm. On a 1:25,000 map, 4 cm is 4 × 250 m = 1000 m, or 1 km.
On a topographic map, grid lines make squares. On a 1:25,000 map, each square is 1 km by 1 km on the ground, so it has an area of 1 square kilometre (1 km²).
To find an area, count the whole squares. Put together the parts of squares to make up whole squares, then add them up. The total is the area in km².
draft.remember: Multiply map centimetres by the scale to get the ground distance. Count grid squares to get area.

a.q: On a map with a scale of 1:25,000, a track measures 6 cm. How long is the track on the ground?
a.why: Each centimetre on the map is 250 m on the ground, so 6 × 250 m = 1500 m, or 1.5 km. Giving 150 m comes from slipping a decimal place when changing 25,000 cm to metres.
a.clue: First work out how many metres 1 cm stands for.

b.q: A national park on a 1:25,000 map covers 5 whole grid squares and parts of squares that join to make 3 more whole squares. Each square is 1 km by 1 km on the ground. What is the area of the park?
b.why: Whole squares and the joined parts give 5 + 3 = 8 squares. Each square is 1 km², so the area is 8 km². Counting only the whole squares gives 5 km², which leaves out the parts of squares.
b.clue: Put the parts of squares together, then count all the squares.
